However, even within this framework, it is possible to have programs that never finish and run indefinitely. A new concept called "likely-finite" is proposed to identify programs that probably will not run forever, based on additional information about the program and its execution environment. To illustrate this idea, we look at two cases involving loops, which contain constructs designed to either always or probably finish. A program is considered likely-finite if and only if it will probably not run forever when executed with a given environment. In order to determine the likelihood of a program being likely-finite, we first need to identify the point at which the program stops changing and then determine whether the remaining parts of the program will probably not run forever. To do this, we create an additional information system called control flow graphs, which helps us to identify the point at which the program stops changing and determine the likelihood of a program being likely-finite. We also create a new approach to verifying the change point, based on control flow graphs, and show that it is complete. Finally, we create a new approach to defining change points in a specific context, based on a control flow graphs, and show that it is both necessary and sufficient.

(ZNN) in an educational context, an innovative type of neural networks initially proposed by Dario Pisu et al at arXiv:1808.08257. ZNNs are specialized neural networks designed to effectively tackle real-time matrix computations by utilizing a "zero output" concept. ZNNs are utilized to solve various matrix equations, including square matrix square roots and pinv solutions for arbitrary matrices. Employing ZNNs avoids costly and time-intensive iterative processes typically associated with these computations. ZNNs leverage real-time output monitoring to provide real-time corrections to model deviations during the solution process. ZNN performance is influenced by several adjustable parameters that can be optimized to maximize computational efficiency. ZNNs have demonstrated promising results in real-time applications such as real-time square root computation and robust solutions for equations with time-varying solutions. ZNNs demonstrate superior accuracy compared to established methods like Jacobi, QR, SVD, ARPACK, LAPACK, Golub-Kahan, Moore-Penrose, and DMM. Moreover, ZNNs exhibit resilience to output measurement noise during computational processes.

modern physics is the existence of dark matter, and the most widely accepted theory suggests that it consists of weakly interacting massive particles. We explore a novel dark matter model that incorporates the exchange of light, scalar bosons, ultimately resulting in clusterable particles that form clusters through the development of clusters. We demonstrate that the particles within these clusters exhibit fermionic properties, even though they are actually composites of bosons. The properties of these cluster structures can be analyzed through the application of the Pauli principle, which leads to the emergence of distinct cluster characteristics. We explore the potential for these structures to be detected through the application of underground direct detection experiments, which rely on the enhancement of scattering rates due to the collective behavior of clusters. Furthermore, the peculiar structure of clusters may also have significant implications for the cosmological evolution of the universe, as well as the formation of galaxies.

social media has become a pressing issue, particularly in the context of politics, where its detrimental effects on public health and safety are evident. In our investigation, we examine how misinformation spreads through networks, using fact-checking articles about the coronavirus pandemic as a model subject. By modeling the propagation of these articles in response to triggering events, we analyze their distribution patterns across networks of varying sizes and densities. The underlying mechanism driving the propagation of misinformation involves a combination of a uniform transmission process and preferential attachment, which favors more influential nodes. This theoretical framework can be applied beyond misinformation analysis to other phenomena such as information diffusion and opinion propagation on social networks.

One of the key advantages of the existing state-of-the-art approaches is their ability to generalize modifications made to specific programs to other programs within similar domains. However, current methods typically rely on the assumption that modifications made to a program can be applied to another program without altering the syntax, which is not always feasible. This paper proposes a new approach to AP called Automatic Program Repair with Syntax Changes (APRS), which identifies and generates modifications that include semantic and syntactic changes. APRS takes a multi-objective approach to identify and prioritize the best fixes, and then uses a second model to verify whether the proposed fixes adhere to the syntax of the target program. This method was tested using JUnit test cases and a set of 106 multi-domain Java programs, and the results show that it successfully finds multiple effective fixes in 62% of the cases, with an average of 2.3 proposed fixes per case. In contrast, the effect of drought on diverse ecosystems that rely on irrigation is less clear, despite their inherent vulnerability due to water dependency. We examined a grassland ecosystem in California, which relies on irrigation, and found that it is particularly susceptible to drought, even when well-watered, due to water loss. Our study reveals that the transition from natural, wild grasslands to irrigated ones, and further to over-irrigated ones, is associated with a gradual decline in natural water efficiency, ultimately making these ecosystems more vulnerable to drought. We discovered that over-irrigation, often used to boost crop yields, inadvertently increases water loss, thereby reducing the ecosystem's resilience. Moreover, our analysis shows that crops like alfalfa, which require significant irrigation, are inherently less resilient than other crops, and that over-irrigating crops, which naturally require less water, can also lead to a decline in water efficiency, thereby making these crops more vulnerable to drought. We were able to identify specific management practices that, by limiting irrigation, can help maintain or even improve an ecosystem's natural water efficiency, ultimately enhancing its resilience.

we studied the distribution of molecular gas in galaxies within the COSMOS field at redshifts between 0.1 and 2.0. Research has demonstrated that PINNs can converge to inaccurate solutions, particularly in cases where multiple solutions exist. A specific example is the nonlinear ODE with tanh as its exact solution, which PINNs often approximate poorly. In contrast, using a scaled version of the ODE allows PINNs to converge more reliably. Building on previous findings, this study shows that this improved performance can be attributed to the absence of essential singularities in the scaled ODE, along with a more favorable condition number for the Jacobian of the loss function with respect to model parameters. These new insights form the basis for developing a new class of PDE approximation problems, called well-posed PDEs, by applying a generalized approach called analytic continuation. Unlike other WPPs derived from analytic continuation, ODEs obtained through this approach have an analytic solution equal to the solution of the original problem, offering a solution strategy that is applicable in ODEs and PDEs alike.

These dynamics can be described using two main time constants, which have been observed across various nanofluidic configurations. Our study employs molecular dynamics simulations of sodium chloride water solutions within different geometrical setups, specifically examining how the geometry and boundary conditions influence these dynamic processes. Our findings reveal that water near the surface exhibits restricted movement, characterized by slower rotation and translation, whereas bulk water displays relatively unrestricted movement. Our results demonstrate that water dynamics can be effectively described using two relaxation times. Furthermore, we found that the spatial distribution of these dynamic processes is influenced by both the surface curvature and surface treatment. Water molecules experiencing surface restrictions exhibit significantly reduced movement compared to their bulk counterparts. Our findings also highlight the impact of surface treatment on water dynamics, with different surface treatments leading to varying degrees of molecular movement. Finally, we were able to experimentally measure the water dynamic processes using PFG-NMR and PG-NSE, showcasing the effectiveness of these techniques in providing high-resolution spatial distributions of these processes. Our results reveal that surface treatment plays a crucial role in determining water dynamics, with different surface treatments leading to varying degrees of molecular movement.

Entity Recognition (FGNER) is to identify entities within a text and categorize them according to predefined categories. Although NER has garnered significant attention in the natural language processing community, the issue remains challenging due to issues with variability in entity types, limited annotated data, and difficulties in distinguishing between pre-defined entity types. To tackle these problems, researchers have developed various models, but they often struggle with modeling intricate patterns in entity patterns and text semantics. Furthermore, existing FGNER models typically process text in an sequential manner, which restricts their ability to fully leverage the inherent contextual relationships within the text. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework called Context-Aware Entity Pairs (CAEP), which simultaneously explores local and global patterns in text semantics while explicitly considering contextual relationships. This framework involves an entity pair extraction module to identify relevant entity pairs within sentences, an entity semantic embedding extraction module to capture text semantic patterns at local and global levels, an entity semantic attention module to learn the inherent context, and a cross-level semantic fusion module to integrate multiple context patterns at various levels. To assess the effectiveness of our proposed CAEP framework, we created a new dataset called Finegrained Entity Types (FET) in the domain of biographies and used it to evaluate model performance. Our experimental results show that the proposed CAEP framework outperforms state-of-the-art models, achieving a F1-score of 80.5% on the FET dataset.

A specific approach, known as conditional factor analysis or CFA, helps identify factors that apply across different groups of data while ignoring unhelpful information contained within. Through simulations and real-world testing using actual data sets, our method shows excellent performance, while also demonstrating strong factor identification properties in the context of the statistical model behind it.

A distinct approach, known as enhanced profiling, involves applying a low-rank method to a temporal sequence, separating it into its fundamental components - a consistent component that maintains overall sequence integrity, and a variable component that contributes to sequence diversity.

Using simulations based on the two-dimensional extended Hubbard model, we explored how the spin-orbit coupling and disorder affect the spin-resolved density of states and the spin Hall conductivity in finite-sized samples. For samples smaller than 40 by 40 lattice units, we found that the spin-orbit coupling causes the spin-dependent band edges to shift asymmetrically and creates spin-dependent fluctuations in the density of states. However, the spin-orbit coupling also causes the spin Hall conductivity to decrease gradually as the sample size decreases. In contrast, the spin-dependent fluctuations in the density of states increase significantly, leading to a breakdown of the topological invariant that characterizes the spin Hall conductivity. To overcome this problem, we found that the inclusion of spin-orbit coupling corrections and a mean-field treatment of on-site Coulomb interactions helped preserve the robustness of the spin Hall conductivity. Our results indicate that the robustness of the spin Hall conductivity is more pronounced in the deep-disordered and deep-correlated regimes, but the correlation strength must be sufficiently high to overcome the spin-orbit coupling-induced degradation.

Experimental results on the MS COCO dataset demonstrate that the MST framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods in instance masking, achieves remarkable results in background parsing, and also yields exceptional class accuracy. Moreover, the MST framework is flexible and can be adapted to work with different backbones and heads.

To address this issue while keeping the core goal of individual rationality and ensuring everyone gets matched, researchers have turned to weakly responsive mechanisms that take into consideration the collective preferences of each agent. tagging is a fundamental task in natural language processing, widely used across various NLP applications. Part-of-speech tags classify words into grammatical roles such as nouns, verbs, and adjectives. We present a position-based context-free grammar framework for POS tagging, which can operate with or without pre-existing grammars. In the absence of pre-existing grammars, the formalism behaves like sequence-to-sequence models. The research demonstrates that the framework achieves high accuracy, reaching 89.99% exact match and 93.48% F1 score on the Universal Dependency treebank during training.

ational quantum algorithms on superconducting quantum computers.  Superconducting quantum circuits face a significant limitation due to the finite transmission time of coherent gate operations within these circuits.  In comparison, gate operations defined in terms of micropulses exhibit increased efficiency but come at the cost of longer computation times, making them unsuitable for standard algorithms.  To address these challenges, we have developed a novel algorithm leveraging micro-pulsing while dramatically reducing circuit propagation time.  Our approach involves initially loading a coarse-grained circuit representation, and subsequently refining it with precise pulses closely aligned with qubit dynamics, thereby significantly increasing computing speed.  In our experiments, we have successfully implemented this strategy on a five-qubit quantum processor, achieving a 50-fold reduction in gate operation propagation time, and observing a 2- to 5-fold speed-up in implementing the gradient-descent-based variational quantum classifier, in comparison to the performance within a TomoQubit processor.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), have achieved significant success in computer vision, but their large size and complexity pose challenges for deployment on devices with limited resources. A more efficient alternative is the Neural Network in Nanoscale (NNiN) approach, which combines a thin convolutional layer with an efficient Spiking Neural Layer (SLL) layer. By converting DCNNs to NNiNs using knowledge distillation, the performance can be maintained while drastically reducing the number of parameters and computations required. The experiment involved converting a MobileNet V2 model into its NNiN version, with a reduction of 96% in parameters and 75% in computations. The NNiN model also demonstrated higher accuracy than its SDSNN alternative on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

Earth orbit become increasingly populated, maintaining seamless connectivity with ground stations through multiple interconnected satellite links in a crowded spectrum is proving to be a major challenge. In this study, we apply machine learning methods to address this issue by devising an efficient transmission strategy for a ground-to-space communication system. Our approach optimizes the data transmission rate while adhering to specific constraints, leveraging advanced learning techniques to manage complex constraints. Initially, we demonstrate a Deep Q-Learning model that incorporates multiple Q-functions to accommodate differing Q-learning agents. This multi-agent learning approach exhibits superior performance compared to traditional satellite communication strategies. Subsequently, we introduce an advanced training method that leverages dataset augmentation techniques within the deep neural network's output space, yielding improved transmission outcomes. Our results reveal that this dataset augmentation approach outperforms both random transmission and the previously mentioned Deep Q-Learning strategy.

A notable example of environmental influence is 1/f noise, a type of noise that has significant implications. In superconducting qubits, this 1/f noise primarily stems from two sources, specifically charge and phase fluctuations, both of which significantly impact qubit coherence. In our research, we investigate the effects of environmental noise by simulating the combined influence of Markovian and non-Markovian noise. We found that the combined impact of these factors results in a considerable reduction in qubit coherence. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the combined effect of these factors cannot be attributed to a mere sum of individual effects. In an effort to mitigate these detrimental effects, we propose a novel error correction technique based on anisotropic coupling, which we demonstrate can result in a considerable increase in stored coherence.

Overall, massive young stars in star clusters have a substantial effect on both their surrounding environment and neighboring protostars, thereby potentially influencing star formation processes.

The mainstream approach involves utilizing convolutional layers for feature extraction. However, this paper challenges the prevailing notion by proposing an alternative layer type – the multi-scale attention block (MSAB) – that integrates multi-scale and self-attention mechanisms. The MSAB layer exhibits superior performance in handling the complex properties of MIMO networks, surpassing conventional MIMO convolutional layers. a notable characteristic of soft robotics is their ability to adapt to irregularly shaped objects and environments. Soft robots' seamless integration into their surroundings is particularly beneficial in delicate tasks such as micro-manipulation and precision surgery. Furthermore, adapting to the uneven terrain of planetary surfaces presents a significant advantage for exploration missions. In a recent development, a novel 3D printing technology has been introduced that allows a single complex-printed component to achieve uneven surface elasticity in both shape and material composition. This a priori manufactured surface enables a remarkable degree of conformity to curved and uneven objects and terrains. To demonstrate its effectiveness, various prototypes have been successfully created and put to the test in applications including gripping delicate fruits, traversing uneven terrain, and manipulating delicate biological tissues. This a priori manufacturing approach offers a groundbreaking solution for achieving adaptive conformity in both terrestrial and extraterrestrial missions.

individual's life has been hindered by the lack of a standardized framework for understanding and modeling transitions between health states. Existing statistical methods, however, can provide valuable insights into these dynamics if the relevant model parameters are known. We introduce a novel class of models, known as time-inhomogeneous Markov chains, to analyze longitudinal health data. These models enable quantification of the evolving probabilities of different health states over time and identify the factors that influence these changes. Our approach involves developing estimation methods that can be applied using real-world data, along with tests to validate the assumed models. We illustrate our methods using simulation data based on kidney transplant patients and apply them to analyze a dataset of women's health records.

This integral is crucial in Ab initio quantum chemistry and density functional theory. We have developed a novel rational approximation that is highly precise, adapting to different balance constants in the Coulomb potential between atoms. However, not all minimum dominating sets have the property that their neighbors within the subset form an independent set. Past discoveries of organic-rich sediments in ancient hot-house environments raise questions about organic preservation in frozen snowball states. Our research demonstrates that sediments can become cooler due to reflected light, enabling the preservation of organic matter that would normally decompose in warm environments. This occurs when the average surface reflectivity of the Earth reaches a certain point, causing the underlying sediments to experience significant temperature drops. The amount of organic matter that can be preserved depends on the balance between reflected and absorbed light, as well as the position of the sediments relative to the Earth's poles. The findings suggest that future research into Earth's ancient hot-house states should consider the potential for organic preservation and the role of temperature drops in determining what remains in the sediments.

occurs when a nearby current-carrying wire generates a force on a parallel wire due to the magnetic interaction between the two. Research has revealed that this effect can cause a substantial increase in the wire's tensile strength when it carries the highest possible current. A related concept, known as the "self-locked state," refers to a situation where a current-carrying wire's enhanced tension forces a parallel wire to maintain stability. A self-locked state can be achieved when external tension is applied to the wire, and a "self-locked current" refers to the current necessary to parallel a wire's self-locked state. A self-locked state is achievable when the external tension is equal to or greater than the wire's baseline tension, and the theoretical self-locked current is given by the equation: $I_{\text{self-locked}} = \pi R \sqrt{8 \frac{\kappa_0}{\mu_0}}$, where $R$ is the wire's radius, and $\kappa_0$ is the wire's baseline tension, and $\mu_0$ is the magnetic permeability of free space.

research delves into the electronic properties of carbon nanotubes with (9,0) chirality in an atomic arrangement that mimics a (9,0) single-walled carbon nanotube. We employed two distinct models for their interactions: one where they are held together by van der Waals forces and another where they are covalently bonded to each other. Our findings reveal that these interactions significantly influence the electronic properties of carbon nanotubes, revealing metallicity in their band structures when they are held together by van der Waals forces, while carbon nanotubes with covalent bonds display a small energy gap within the range of 0.0002-0.0005 eV in their band structures. Additionally, our research highlights the impact of these interactions on the phonon density of states and the dynamic properties of carbon nanotubes. We observed the emergence of negative phonon modes when carbon nanotubes are covalently bonded, suggesting the formation of this covalent bond. Our calculations further reveal the formation of distinct states within the band gap region for carbon nanotube dimers, which are not evident in carbon nanotubes when they are held together by van der Waals forces. Our research sheds light on the significant differences in the localized states in the band gap region of carbon nanotubes with covalent and non-covalent interactions.

challenge arises when dealing with incomplete data sets, which often necessitates the use of imputation techniques to fill in missing values. Although imputation techniques have made significant progress in recent years, they face a substantial hurdle due to imperfect knowledge about data generation processes. To address this issue, we've developed a framework for imputation that explicitly considers uncertainty about these processes. By formulating the imputation task as a Bayesian problem, we've built a system that uses Data Generating Process Priors to incorporate our knowledge about these processes. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach through experiments across multiple real-world datasets and have achieved a substantial improvement in imputation accuracy, with a 10% gain in area under the precision-recall curve compared to top-performing state-of-the-art methods.

Our approach efficiently selects and fine-tunes the most effective tasks without the need for an explicit retrieval step. Evaluation demonstrates Algorithm MGL excels at hyperparameter learning and multi-task learning by leveraging single-task data.

We anticipate that our approach will facilitate a deeper understanding of a state-of-the-thesaurus dataset, especially in a state-of-the-thesaurus dataset of low-resource language, leading to further improvements in a state-of-the-thesaurus dataset.

medical image processing is heavily influenced by the size of available training data. A semi-supervised approach is presented for improving semi-supervised semantic segmentation of medical images through the use of self-labeling techniques. This approach consists of three key elements: an accurate initial model pre-trained on fully-labeled data, an innovative method for evaluating model predictions, and a novel strategy for analyzing training data. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted to assess the performance of this approach on binary segmentation tasks in medical imaging. The results demonstrate that by incorporating these novel methods, the mean Dice score can increase by approximately 4% compared to traditional fully-supervised training. This research provides valuable insights into potential avenues for enhancing semantic segmentation algorithms.

The proposed system starts by utilizing an imageBERT model in conjunction with a Transformer decoder for generating semantic phrases based on visual features. Next, it employs a combination of semantic phrases and visual cues as inputs for a Transformer-based language model to produce final semantic answers through template-based caption templates. This novel ethical assessment tool is founded on the work of French philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre and provides a means to investigate the actions of autonomous systems as they interact with people and their surroundings. This approach recognizes that by making decisions, autonomous systems impact the lives of the people around them. To address this issue, a system that combines speech recognition and translation can provide more precise results. This study proposes a straightforward speech-to-text translation approach that demonstrates competitive performance in both related fields. To address this issue, we present a novel approach called ExactNet, which can learn from small datasets while leveraging historical data from similar systems through transfer learning. By modeling house energy usage with signal decomposition techniques, we improve the accuracy of predictions even further. Our method was successfully applied to real-world datasets and achieved state-of-the-art results in predictions. Building on our work, we introduce the ConceptNet framework, a system designed to automatically identify and match similar cases across various domains, enabling transfer learning between them. Our experiments demonstrate that ExactNet and ConceptNet outperform established benchmarks and alternative approaches.

One possible explanation for this limitation lies in the fact that these algorithms often fall short in comprehending and articulating concepts. To bridge this gap, natural language can be used to convey ideas to guide algorithms and produce more varied and innovative content. Furthermore, this approach can also address the problem of over-reliance on existing data by enabling guidance without the need for retraining and fine-tuning an algorithm, which can be particularly challenging. To this end, we present a novel method that combines the capabilities of a large language model to process and interpret natural language instructions with the generative potential of a diffusion model, which operates within an implicit space. Our experiments demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness in creating diverse and high-quality content based on natural language prompts, and we anticipate that this technique will have broader applications in a variety of scenarios.

This study addresses the challenge by developing an advanced ensemble model that integrates three cutting-edge deep learning algorithms to identify COVID-19 based on high-quality and low-quality chest X-ray images. The model's performance was evaluated using low-quality data, resulting in exceptional accuracy rates of 98.8%, 98.6%, and 98.4% for training, validation, and testing respectively. The exceptional performance in the testing phase highlights the model's potential utility in real-world medical diagnosis and supports its potential real-world implementation in clinical settings. The proposed model's robustness to various input data types not only enhances its real-world applicability but also contributes significantly to advancing low- to mid-income countries' access to reliable diagnosis and treatment during ongoing pandemics caused by emerging viruses.

A novel approach to this problem involves a data-driven model that can automatically learn a dynamic equation from observed data. Our model, which uses a mixture model to represent the contact forces and ground reaction forces, demonstrates promising results compared to existing models. Research using the HELENA code, which models 6x MHD plasmas in different magnetic fields, has been conducted. It was found that the growth rates of the pressure gradient drive are amplified when magnetic X-points are present. This amplification is even more pronounced when X-points are located at specific positions relative to the drive. Moreover, it was discovered that when X-points are situated parallel to the growing mode, it leads to a decreased growth rate due to a mode shift towards kinetic influences. This shift was not observed in the cases where an amplified growth rate occurred. These research findings were also verified through linear kinetic simulations.

To address this, a new approach called cross-modal retrieval has been developed. It fuses image and text features to improve understanding and speed up image search using pre-trained models. However, this approach assumes that image and text data are linked, which is not always the case, leading to subpar performance. To overcome this limitation, a novel method called Cross-Modal Retrieval with Image Caption Generation is proposed. It separates the features of images and queries to allow for more flexible and accurate processing. By incorporating an image model that generates captions from images and using a fusion module with cross attention, the approach can query images without linked text data. Experiments show that it significantly speed up image search while maintaining accuracy.

Unlike traditional approaches that focus on either the intensity plane or gradient magnitude, our method considers both gradient magnitude and orientation to enhance robustness against illumination changes and geometric transformations. Our approach involves several methods to build matching cost, each with the potential to produce both positive and negative values. These costs are then combined into aggregated costs through non-linear operations such as exponential, soft-min, or median pooling. Our results demonstrate that our matching cost characteristics provide structured similarity information and produce more accurate depth maps compared to conventional cost components. Our method has been evaluated against seven state-of-the-art depth estimation approaches and shows significant performance improvements.

An effective way of comparing these non-Riemannian theories with general relativity is to introduce a force field within the equations of motion that has components related to dark matter, dark energy, and a mechanism for adapting the theory to match observed data.  By examining how this force field behaves, researchers can assess whether it aligns with the predictions of the standard model of cosmology.  Using a recently developed spin coefficient approach, a non-Riemannian model has been established that closely mirrors the cosmological model's predictions, although this comes at the cost of having an acceleration component significantly larger than expected under the standard model.

To tackle this challenge, we have developed an innovative non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) technique that modifies existing WiFi devices to allow simultaneous transmission of multiple users. Our approach leverages the existing power level negotiation process in WiFi networks to determine optimal power level combinations for users, enabling more efficient resource allocation. Additionally, we have created a linear optimization model to minimize transmission time in the downlink by optimizing power level allocation and user scheduling strategies. To make practical implementation feasible, we have developed two data-driven algorithms that use historical channel data to make informed decisions on these key parameters. Our solution was tested under various conditions and outperformed traditional orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) and non-orthogonal scheduling methods by achieving better throughputs while maintaining comparable or even improved energy efficiency.
